title: Clamped Health Points
prompt_md:
## Goal
Define a `Hero` class whose health points can never leave the range [0, maxHp], no matter what callers do. Because the HP member is private and only reachable through your member functions, the class itself becomes the single place responsible for keeping that invariant true.

## Input
Three integers on separate lines: the hero's maximum HP, an amount of damage to apply, then an amount to heal. The hero begins at full HP. Apply the damage first, then the heal.

## Output
Two lines: `HP after damage: <value>` and `HP after heal: <value>`, each clamped to [0, maxHp].

## Feature
This exercises data hiding / encapsulation: a private invariant (0 <= HP <= maxHp) enforced by every mutator, so no outside code can put the object into an invalid state. Initialize the hero through a public setter (constructors come later).

test_cases.label: Sample: normal damage and heal
test_cases.expected_stdout:
HP after damage: 70
HP after heal: 90

test_cases.label: Hidden: damage exceeds maxHp
test_cases.expected_stdout:
HP after damage: 0
HP after heal: 10

test_cases.label: Hidden: heal capped at max HP
test_cases.expected_stdout:
HP after damage: 100
HP after heal: 100

title: Distance Behind an Interface
prompt_md:
## Goal
Define a `Distance` class that stores its length internally in millimeters but presents a centimeter-based interface to callers. The choice of internal unit is hidden behind the public functions, so it could change later without any caller noticing.

## Input
One integer: a length in centimeters.

## Output
Two lines: `cm: <value>` (the length in whole centimeters) and `mm: <value>` (the same length in millimeters).

## Feature
This exercises the maintainability benefit of data hiding: the public interface (centimeters) is decoupled from the private representation (millimeters), so the stored unit is an implementation detail callers never depend on.
